title: Coordination Compounds
tagline: Werner's theory, nomenclature, isomerism, bonding theories and applications of coordination compounds in the ISC XII syllabus.

overview.intro: Coordination compounds are compounds in which a central metal atom or ion is surrounded by a number of ions or molecules, called ligands, that donate electron pairs to it. They include many of the most important substances in chemistry and biology, from haemoglobin and chlorophyll to industrial catalysts and analytical reagents. The central ideas are the coordination number, which is the number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal, and the distinction between the coordination sphere, written in square brackets, and the ions outside it. Werner's coordination theory explained the existence of such compounds by postulating two types of valency, and modern bonding theories describe the metal-ligand interaction in terms of valence bond theory and crystal field theory. This chapter covers the terminology and nomenclature of coordination compounds, the main types of isomerism they exhibit, the bonding models used to explain their shapes, colours and magnetic properties, and their stability and applications in qualitative analysis, extraction of metals, biological systems and medicine.

learn.title: Terminology, ligands and Werner's coordination theory

blocks.text: A coordination compound consists of a central metal atom or ion bonded to a set of surrounding ions or molecules called ligands. The ligands donate electron pairs to the metal, forming coordinate bonds, and the atom in the ligand that provides the electron pair is the donor atom. The coordination number is the number of donor atoms directly attached to the metal, not necessarily the number of ligand molecules, because a single ligand may bind through more than one donor atom. The coordination sphere is the central metal together with its ligands and is written inside square brackets; species outside the brackets are counter ions that balance the charge. The oxidation state of the metal is found by treating the ligands as if they were removed with their donor pairs and assigning charges accordingly.

Ligands are classified by denticity. Monodentate ligands such as water, ammonia and chloride bind through one donor atom. Bidentate ligands such as ethylenediamine and oxalate bind through two donor atoms, and polydentate ligands such as EDTA bind through several, forming ring structures called chelates. Ambidentate ligands such as nitrite and thiocyanate can bind through different donor atoms, giving linkage isomers. Werner proposed in 1893 that metals in coordination compounds exhibit two types of valency: a primary valency, which corresponds to the oxidation state and is satisfied by negative ions and is ionisable, and a secondary valency, which corresponds to the coordination number, is satisfied by ligands, is directional and determines the geometry of the complex. His theory explained why compounds such as CoCl3.6NH3 behave differently from CoCl3.5NH3 in precipitation reactions with silver nitrate.

items.meaning: An ion or molecule that donates one or more electron pairs to a central metal atom or ion to form a coordinate bond.
The number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal atom or ion.
The central metal and its attached ligands, written together inside square brackets.
The number of donor atoms in a ligand that bind to the central metal in a single coordination entity.
A complex in which a polydentate ligand forms one or more rings by binding to the metal through two or more donor atoms.

items.text: In [Co(NH3)6]Cl3, identify the coordination sphere, the coordination number and the oxidation state of cobalt.
items.note: The coordination sphere is [Co(NH3)6]3+, containing six ammonia ligands bonded to cobalt, so the coordination number is 6. The three chloride ions outside balance a +3 charge, and since ammonia is neutral, the oxidation state of cobalt is +3.

items.text: Why does [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 give two moles of AgCl with excess silver nitrate, while [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 gives three?
items.note: Only the chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are ionisable. The first compound has two chloride ions outside and one inside bonded to cobalt, so it precipitates two moles of AgCl. The second has all three outside, so it precipitates three.

blocks.text: The IUPAC name of a coordination compound is built systematically from the names of the ligands and the metal. Ligands are named first, in alphabetical order ignoring numerical prefixes, followed by the name of the central metal. Anionic ligands end in -o, for example chloro, cyano and oxalato, neutral ligands usually keep their names with a few exceptions such as aqua for water, ammine for ammonia and carbonyl for carbon monoxide. Numerical prefixes di, tri, tetra, penta and hexa indicate the number of each ligand, but when the ligand name already contains a numerical prefix, bis, tris and tetrakis are used instead. The oxidation state of the metal is given in Roman numerals in parentheses immediately after the metal name.

If the coordination entity is a cation or a neutral molecule, the metal keeps its usual name. If the coordination entity is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate, often using the Latin root, for example ferrate for iron, cuprate for copper and argentate for silver. In writing formulae, the central metal is written first within the coordination sphere, followed by the ligands in alphabetical order of their symbols, and the entire coordination sphere is enclosed in square brackets. Counter ions are written outside the brackets, cations before and anions after.

items: Name ligands alphabetically before the metal, ignoring di, tri, tetra and similar prefixes.
Anionic ligands end in -o: chloro, bromo, cyano, hydroxo, oxalato, carbonato.
Neutral ligands: aqua (H2O), ammine (NH3), carbonyl (CO), nitrosyl (NO).
Use bis, tris, tetrakis when the ligand name already includes a numerical prefix, as in ethylenediamine.
Cationic or neutral complex: metal keeps its name; anionic complex: metal name ends in -ate.
Oxidation state of the metal is shown in Roman numerals in parentheses.

items.note: Five ammine ligands and one chloro ligand are named alphabetically as pentaamminechloro, the complex is a cation so cobalt keeps its name, and the oxidation state is +3. The name is pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride.

items.text: Write the formula for potassium hexacyanoferrate(II).
items.note: Hexacyano indicates six cyanide ligands, ferrate(II) indicates an anionic iron complex with iron in the +2 state, giving [Fe(CN)6]4-. Four potassium ions balance the charge, so the formula is K4[Fe(CN)6].

blocks.text: Isomers are compounds with the same formula but different arrangements of atoms, and coordination compounds show a rich variety of isomerism. Structural isomerism arises when the connectivity differs. Ionisation isomerism occurs when an ion inside the coordination sphere exchanges places with a counter ion, giving compounds that produce different ions in solution, such as [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br. Hydrate or solvate isomerism is a related case in which water molecules may be inside or outside the coordination sphere. Linkage isomerism occurs with ambidentate ligands, for example nitrite binding through nitrogen as nitro or through oxygen as nitrito. Coordination isomerism occurs when both cation and anion are complex ions and ligands are exchanged between them.

Stereoisomerism arises when the connectivity is the same but the spatial arrangement differs. Geometrical isomerism occurs in square planar and octahedral complexes when ligands can occupy different relative positions. In a square planar complex of the type [Ma2b2], the two identical ligands may be adjacent, giving the cis isomer, or opposite, giving the trans isomer. In octahedral complexes, [Ma4b2] shows cis and trans forms, and [Ma3b3] shows facial (fac) and meridional (mer) forms. Optical isomerism occurs when a complex and its mirror image are not superimposable; this is common in octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands such as [Co(en)3]3+, which exists as a pair of enantiomers.

items: Ionisation isomers give different ions in solution and therefore different precipitation reactions.
Hydrate isomers differ in the number of water molecules inside and outside the coordination sphere.
Linkage isomers arise from ambidentate ligands such as NO2- (nitro or nitrito) and SCN- (thiocyanato or isothiocyanato).
Coordination isomers involve exchange of ligands between cationic and anionic complex ions.
Geometrical isomerism: cis and trans in square planar and octahedral complexes, fac and mer in [Ma3b3].
Optical isomerism requires non-superimposable mirror images, common in complexes with chelating ligands.

items.text: Identify the type of isomerism shown by [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2 and [Co(NH3)5(ONO)]Cl2.
items.note: The nitrite ligand binds through nitrogen in the first complex and through oxygen in the second, so the two are linkage isomers. They have the same formula but different connectivity.

items.text: Why does cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2] show geometrical isomerism while [Pt(NH3)4]Cl2 does not?
items.note: In cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2] the two chloride ligands can be adjacent or opposite in the square planar arrangement, giving cis and trans forms. In [Pt(NH3)4]2+ all four ligands are identical, so no distinct spatial arrangements are possible.

learn.title: Valence bond theory and crystal field theory

blocks.text: Valence bond theory describes bonding in coordination compounds as the overlap of filled ligand orbitals with vacant hybrid orbitals on the metal. The geometry of the complex is determined by the type of hybridisation: sp3 gives tetrahedral, dsp2 gives square planar, sp3d2 gives outer orbital octahedral and d2sp3 gives inner orbital octahedral. The magnetic behaviour follows from the number of unpaired electrons remaining after hybridisation. Strong field ligands such as CN- can force pairing of d electrons, leading to low-spin inner orbital complexes, while weak field ligands such as F- leave electrons unpaired, leading to high-spin outer orbital complexes. Valence bond theory successfully predicts geometry and magnetic properties in many cases but does not explain colour or the relative stabilities of complexes.

Crystal field theory treats the metal-ligand interaction as purely electrostatic. In an octahedral complex the six ligands approach along the axes, raising the energy of the dx2-y2 and dz2 orbitals, which point towards the ligands, relative to the dxy, dxz and dyz orbitals, which point between them. The d orbitals split into a lower t2g set and a higher eg set separated by the crystal field splitting energy delta_o. If delta_o is large, as with strong field ligands, electrons pair in the t2g orbitals before occupying eg, giving a low-spin complex; if delta_o is small, electrons occupy all orbitals singly before pairing, giving a high-spin complex. The absorption of light corresponding to the energy gap delta_o explains the colour of coordination compounds, and the magnitude of delta_o depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the position of the ligand in the spectrochemical series.

items.text: Explain why [CoF6]3- is paramagnetic while [Co(NH3)6]3+ is diamagnetic.
items.note: Both contain Co3+ with a 3d6 configuration. Fluoride is a weak field ligand, so in [CoF6]3- the splitting is small, electrons remain unpaired and the complex is paramagnetic with sp3d2 hybridisation. Ammonia is a stronger field ligand, so in [Co(NH3)6]3+ the splitting is large, electrons pair in the t2g orbitals and the complex is diamagnetic with d2sp3 hybridisation.

learn.title: Stability and applications of coordination compounds

blocks.text: The stability of a coordination compound in solution refers to the extent to which the complex resists dissociation into the metal ion and ligands. It is expressed quantitatively by the stability constant or formation constant: a larger value indicates a more stable complex. Stability depends on the nature of the metal ion, including its charge and size, and on the nature of the ligand. Chelating ligands form more stable complexes than comparable monodentate ligands, an effect known as the chelate effect, because the formation of rings increases the entropy of the system and makes dissociation less favourable. Strong field ligands and ligands that form multiple bonds with the metal also tend to give more stable complexes.

Coordination compounds have wide applications. In qualitative analysis, complexes are used to detect and separate metal ions, for example the formation of Prussian blue with iron and the use of dimethylglyoxime to detect nickel. In the extraction and purification of metals, complexes such as [Ag(CN)2]- and [Au(CN)2]- are used in the cyanide process, and nickel is purified by forming volatile Ni(CO)4 in the Mond process. In biological systems, haemoglobin is an iron coordination complex that transports oxygen, chlorophyll is a magnesium complex essential for photosynthesis, and vitamin B12 contains cobalt. In medicine, cisplatin is a platinum coordination compound used in cancer treatment, and EDTA is used to treat lead poisoning by forming a stable chelate that can be excreted.

items: Stability constant measures the equilibrium between a complex and its dissociated metal ion and ligands.
The chelate effect makes complexes with polydentate ligands more stable than those with similar monodentate ligands.
Hard and soft acid-base considerations also influence stability: hard metals prefer hard donors such as oxygen, soft metals prefer soft donors such as sulphur.
Analytical applications include detection of Ni2+ with dimethylglyoxime and Fe3+ with thiocyanate.
Metallurgical applications include the Mond process for nickel and cyanide leaching for gold and silver.
Biological examples include haemoglobin (iron), chlorophyll (magnesium) and vitamin B12 (cobalt).

items.text: Why is [Ni(en)3]2+ more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]2+ even though both have six nitrogen donor atoms?
items.note: Ethylenediamine is a bidentate ligand that forms chelate rings with the metal. The chelate effect increases the stability of the complex because forming rings is entropically favoured compared with binding six separate ammonia molecules.

items.text: Explain the role of EDTA in the treatment of lead poisoning.
items.note: EDTA is a hexadentate ligand that forms a very stable chelate complex with Pb2+ ions. Once complexed, the lead is held tightly and can be excreted from the body, reducing its toxic effects.

keyPoints: A coordination compound consists of a central metal atom or ion bonded to ligands that donate electron pairs.
The coordination number is the number of donor atoms directly attached to the metal, and the coordination sphere is written in square brackets.
Werner's theory distinguishes primary valency (oxidation state, ionisable) from secondary valency (coordination number, directional).
IUPAC names list ligands alphabetically before the metal, with the oxidation state in Roman numerals.
Structural isomerism includes ionisation, hydrate, linkage and coordination isomerism; stereoisomerism includes geometrical and optical isomerism.
Valence bond theory explains geometry and magnetic behaviour using hybridisation such as sp3, dsp2, sp3d2 and d2sp3.
Crystal field theory explains colour and magnetic properties through splitting of d orbitals into t2g and eg sets in an octahedral field.
Strong field ligands produce larger splitting and favour low-spin complexes; weak field ligands favour high-spin complexes.
The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by increasing field strength from iodide to carbon monoxide.
Chelating ligands increase stability through the chelate effect.
Coordination compounds are important in analysis, metallurgy, biological systems and medicine.
examFocus: Determining the oxidation state, coordination number and denticity in a given coordination compound.
Writing IUPAC names from formulae and formulae from names.
Identifying types of isomerism and drawing or describing cis, trans, fac and mer forms.
Predicting geometry and magnetic behaviour using valence bond theory and hybridisation.
Explaining colour and high-spin versus low-spin behaviour using crystal field splitting.
Using the spectrochemical series to compare ligand field strengths.
Describing the chelate effect and giving examples of applications in biology and medicine.

An ion or molecule that donates one or more electron pairs to the central metal atom or ion.
The number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal atom or ion.
The central metal and its attached ligands, enclosed in square brackets in the formula.
The number of donor atoms through which a ligand binds to the central metal.
A complex formed when a polydentate ligand binds through two or more donor atoms to create ring structures.
A ligand that can coordinate through two different donor atoms, though only one at a time.
Stereoisomerism arising from different spatial arrangements of ligands, such as cis and trans forms.
Stereoisomerism in which isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

questions.prompt: The coordination number of cobalt in [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is:
questions.answer: six
questions.explanation: Six ammonia molecules are directly bonded to the cobalt ion inside the coordination sphere, so the coordination number is 6. The three chloride ions outside are counter ions and do not count towards the coordination number.
questions.commonMistake: Adding the counter ions to the number of ligands.

questions.prompt: Which of the following ligands is bidentate?
questions.answer: Ethylenediamine
questions.explanation: Ethylenediamine has two nitrogen donor atoms and can bind to the metal through both, forming a chelate ring. Ammonia, chloride and water are monodentate ligands that bind through a single donor atom.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming a larger ligand must be bidentate without checking the number of donor atoms.

questions.prompt: The IUPAC name of K4[Fe(CN)6] is:
questions.answer: Potassium hexacyanoferrate(II)
questions.explanation: The complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4- is an anion, so the metal is named ferrate. Six cyanide ligands give a total charge of -6, and the overall charge is -4, so iron is in the +2 oxidation state.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to use the -ate ending for a metal in an anionic complex.

questions.prompt: The compounds [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br are examples of:
questions.answer: Ionisation isomerism
questions.explanation: The bromide and sulphate ions exchange positions between the coordination sphere and the outside, so the two compounds give different ions in solution and precipitate different ions with reagents.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing ionisation isomerism with coordination isomerism.

questions.prompt: According to crystal field theory, in an octahedral complex the d orbitals split into:
options: a lower-energy t2g set and a higher-energy eg set
a lower-energy eg set and a higher-energy t2g set
five orbitals each with a different energy
questions.answer: a lower-energy t2g set and a higher-energy eg set
questions.explanation: In an octahedral field the ligands approach along the axes, raising the energy of the dx2-y2 and dz2 orbitals (eg) more than the dxy, dxz and dyz orbitals (t2g), which point between the axes.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the order of the t2g and eg sets.

questions.prompt: A complex that contains unpaired electrons is:
questions.answer: paramagnetic
questions.explanation: Unpaired electrons give rise to a net magnetic moment, so the complex is attracted into a magnetic field and is described as paramagnetic. Diamagnetic complexes have all electrons paired.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that all coordination compounds are paramagnetic.

questions.prompt: Which of the following ligands produces the strongest crystal field splitting according to the spectrochemical series?
questions.answer: CN-
questions.explanation: In the spectrochemical series, cyanide is a strong field ligand that produces a large crystal field splitting, much greater than water, fluoride or chloride. Strong field ligands favour low-spin complexes.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing halide ions, which are weak field ligands.

questions.prompt: The greater stability of [Ni(en)3]2+ compared with [Ni(NH3)6]2+ is due to:
options: the larger size of ammonia molecules
the higher oxidation state of nickel
questions.answer: the chelate effect
questions.explanation: Ethylenediamine is a bidentate ligand that forms chelate rings with the metal. The formation of these rings is entropically favoured, making the complex more stable than the analogous complex with monodentate ammonia ligands.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the stability difference to a change in coordination number.

questions.prompt: Ligands that can bind to a metal through two or more donor atoms are called ______ ligands.
questions.answer: polydentate
questions.explanation: Polydentate ligands such as ethylenediamine and EDTA have more than one donor atom and can form chelate rings with the central metal ion.
questions.commonMistake: Writing ambidentate, which refers to a ligand that can bind through different atoms but only one at a time.

questions.prompt: In the IUPAC name of an anionic coordination complex, the name of the metal ends with the suffix ______.
questions.answer: -ate
questions.explanation: When the coordination entity is an anion, the metal is given an -ate ending, often using a Latin root, such as ferrate for iron and cuprate for copper.
questions.commonMistake: Using the normal metal name without the -ate suffix.

questions.prompt: Isomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other are called ______ isomers.
questions.answer: optical
questions.explanation: Optical isomers, or enantiomers, rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions and occur in coordination compounds that lack a plane of symmetry, such as [Co(en)3]3+.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing optical isomerism with geometrical isomerism.

questions.prompt: State Werner's postulates regarding the two types of valency in coordination compounds.
questions.answer: Werner proposed that metals in coordination compounds exhibit a primary valency and a secondary valency. The primary valency corresponds to the oxidation state of the metal, is satisfied by negative ions and is ionisable. The secondary valency corresponds to the coordination number, is satisfied by ligands, is non-ionisable and is directional, determining the geometry of the complex.
questions.explanation: These postulates explained why some ions in a coordination compound are precipitated by reagents while others are not, and why complexes have definite geometries.
questions.commonMistake: Treating both valencies as ionisable or as non-directional.

questions.prompt: Write the IUPAC name of [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl.
questions.answer: The complex contains four aqua ligands and two chloro ligands, named alphabetically as tetraaquadichlorido. The coordination entity is a cation and the oxidation state of chromium is +3, so the name is tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) chloride.
questions.explanation: Alphabetical order is based on the ligand names aqua and chlorido, and the oxidation state is found by balancing the charges of two chloride ligands and one counter ion against the neutral water ligands.
questions.commonMistake: Calculating the oxidation state as +2 by forgetting the chloride ion outside the coordination sphere.

questions.prompt: What is linkage isomerism? Give one example.
questions.answer: Linkage isomerism occurs when an ambidentate ligand can coordinate to the central metal through two different donor atoms, giving complexes with the same formula but different connectivity. An example is [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2, in which nitrite binds through nitrogen, and [Co(NH3)5(ONO)]Cl2, in which it binds through oxygen.
questions.explanation: The ligand itself is the same, but the atom attached to the metal differs, which can lead to different colours and chemical properties.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing linkage isomerism with ionisation isomerism.

questions.prompt: Explain why [Ni(CN)4]2- is square planar and diamagnetic while [NiCl4]2- is tetrahedral and paramagnetic.
questions.answer: In [Ni(CN)4]2-, cyanide is a strong field ligand that causes pairing of the 3d electrons of Ni2+, allowing dsp2 hybridisation and giving a square planar, diamagnetic complex with no unpaired electrons. In [NiCl4]2-, chloride is a weak field ligand that does not cause pairing, so the complex uses sp3 hybridisation, giving a tetrahedral geometry with two unpaired electrons and paramagnetic behaviour.
questions.explanation: The difference in geometry and magnetic property arises from the different field strengths of the ligands, which determine whether electron pairing occurs before hybridisation.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that all four-coordinate nickel complexes have the same geometry.

questions.prompt: Describe the types of structural isomerism shown by coordination compounds, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Ionisation isomerism occurs when a counter ion and a ligand inside the coordination sphere exchange places, as in [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br, which give different ions in solution. Hydrate or solvate isomerism occurs when water molecules differ in being inside or outside the coordination sphere, as in [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 and [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O. Linkage isomerism occurs with ambidentate ligands that can bind through different donor atoms, as in [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2 and [Co(NH3)5(ONO)]Cl2. Coordination isomerism occurs when both cation and anion are complexes and ligands are exchanged between them, as in [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] and [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6].
questions.explanation: All these forms of isomerism involve the same overall composition but different connectivity or different distribution of species between the coordination sphere and the outside.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one type of structural isomerism or confusing it with stereoisomerism.

questions.prompt: Explain crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes and show how it accounts for high-spin and low-spin configurations.
questions.answer: In an octahedral complex, six ligands approach the central metal ion along the x, y and z axes. The d orbitals that point along these axes, dx2-y2 and dz2, experience greater repulsion and are raised in energy to form the eg set, while the dxy, dxz and dyz orbitals point between the axes and form the lower-energy t2g set. The energy difference is the crystal field splitting energy delta_o. When delta_o is small, as with weak field ligands, electrons occupy all five d orbitals singly before pairing, giving a high-spin complex with more unpaired electrons. When delta_o is large, as with strong field ligands, electrons pair in the lower t2g orbitals before occupying eg, giving a low-spin complex with fewer unpaired electrons.
questions.explanation: The balance between the pairing energy and the crystal field splitting energy determines whether a complex is high spin or low spin, which in turn affects its magnetic properties and colour.
questions.commonMistake: Placing the eg orbitals at lower energy than the t2g orbitals in an octahedral field.

questions.prompt: Discuss the applications of coordination compounds in biological systems and in medicine, giving specific examples.
questions.answer: Coordination compounds play essential roles in biological systems. Haemoglobin is an iron(II) coordination complex in which the iron is bound to a porphyrin ring and can reversibly bind oxygen for transport in the blood. Chlorophyll is a magnesium coordination complex that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis, and vitamin B12 is a cobalt coordination compound required for red blood cell formation and nerve function. In medicine, cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2], is used as an anticancer drug because it binds to DNA and interferes with cell division in tumour cells. EDTA is used in chelation therapy to treat heavy metal poisoning by forming stable, water-soluble complexes with toxic metal ions such as lead so that they can be excreted from the body.
questions.explanation: In each case the biological or therapeutic function depends on the ability of the metal centre to bind specific ligands in a defined geometry, which is the characteristic feature of coordination chemistry.
questions.commonMistake: Giving general statements about metals in the body without naming specific coordination compounds and their roles.

questions.prompt: For the complex [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl, determine the oxidation state of cobalt, the coordination number and the number of ions produced in aqueous solution.
questions.answer: Let the oxidation state of cobalt be x. Ammonia is neutral and each chloride has charge -1, so x + 0 + 2(-1) + (-1) = 0, giving x = +3. The coordination sphere contains four ammonia molecules and two chloride ions directly bonded to cobalt, so the coordination number is 6. In aqueous solution the complex dissociates into [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ and one Cl- ion, producing two ions in total.
questions.explanation: Only the chloride ion outside the coordination sphere is ionisable. The two chloride ions inside are coordinated to cobalt and do not dissociate in solution.
questions.commonMistake: Counting all three chloride ions as ionisable or taking the coordination number as 4.

questions.prompt: Using valence bond theory, predict the hybridisation, geometry and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CN)4]2-.
questions.answer: Nickel in [Ni(CN)4]2- is in the +2 oxidation state with configuration 3d8. Cyanide is a strong field ligand and causes pairing of the two unpaired 3d electrons, leaving one 3d orbital vacant. The complex then uses dsp2 hybridisation involving one 3d, one 4s and two 4p orbitals, giving a square planar geometry. Since all electrons are paired after hybridisation, the complex is diamagnetic.
questions.explanation: The strong field cyanide ligands force electron pairing, which makes an inner d orbital available for hybridisation and leads to the characteristic square planar geometry of many d8 complexes.
questions.commonMistake: Predicting sp3 hybridisation and tetrahedral geometry without considering the effect of strong field ligands.

questions.prompt: A coordination compound has the empirical formula CoCl3.4NH3. One mole of this compound gives one mole of AgCl when treated with excess silver nitrate solution. Write the structural formula of the compound, give its IUPAC name and state its coordination number and the oxidation state of cobalt.
questions.answer: Since only one mole of AgCl is formed, only one chloride ion is outside the coordination sphere and the other two are bonded to cobalt. The structural formula is [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl. Its IUPAC name is tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride. The coordination number is 6 because four ammonia molecules and two chloride ions are directly bonded to cobalt. The oxidation state of cobalt is +3, found by balancing four neutral ammonia ligands and three chloride ions with total charge -3 against the neutral compound.
questions.explanation: The precipitation test with silver nitrate reveals how many chloride ions are ionisable, which identifies which ligands are inside the coordination sphere. This is a direct application of Werner's distinction between primary and secondary valencies.
questions.commonMistake: Placing all three chloride ions outside the coordination sphere despite the precipitation data.

questions.prompt: Explain, using crystal field theory, why [Fe(H2O)6]3+ is paramagnetic while [Fe(CN)6]3- is also paramagnetic but with fewer unpaired electrons. State the number of unpaired electrons in each complex.
questions.answer: Both complexes contain Fe3+ with a 3d5 configuration. Water is a weak field ligand, so in [Fe(H2O)6]3+ the crystal field splitting is small and the five d electrons occupy all orbitals singly before pairing, giving a high-spin complex with five unpaired electrons. Cyanide is a strong field ligand, so in [Fe(CN)6]3- the splitting is large and electrons pair in the lower t2g orbitals before occupying eg, giving a low-spin t2g5 configuration with one unpaired electron. Both complexes are therefore paramagnetic, but [Fe(H2O)6]3+ has a much larger magnetic moment than [Fe(CN)6]3-.
questions.explanation: The difference arises because the pairing energy is compared with the crystal field splitting: when the splitting exceeds the pairing energy, pairing occurs and the number of unpaired electrons decreases.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that a strong field ligand always produces a diamagnetic complex, which is not true for a d5 ion with an odd number of electrons.
